results.claim: Every connected cograph other than a singleton or a graph with exactly one universal vertex is equivalent to the zero game.
results.proof_sketch: Let C be connected. Its cotree root is a join. If C has at least two universal vertices, pairing any two of them is a pairing dominating set, so C=0 by Remark 9. If C has no universal vertex, every root-join block has at least two vertices. Choose distinct a,b in one block and c,d in another. The disjoint pairs (a,b),(c,d) dominate C in the pairing sense: vertices in the first block lie in N[c]∩N[d], while all other vertices lie in N[a]∩N[b]. Hence C=0. The only remaining connected cases are K1 and components having a unique universal vertex.

results.claim: SHVG on cographs is polynomially equivalent to an explicit open-or-delete scoring game on rooted forests.
results.proof_sketch:
Construct a forest R(G) recursively over connected components. Ignore zero components from the preceding claim. A K1 component becomes a prize leaf. If a nontrivial component C has unique universal vertex u, make an internal root whose children are R(C-u).

Moves at u dominate other moves in C. For Maker, transpose u with any proposed first move x in a simulated strategy. If simulated u ultimately belongs to Maker, the final coloring is unchanged on {u,x}; if simulated u belongs to Breaker, the simulated contribution of C is zero while the transposed contribution is nonnegative. The analogous transposition proves dominance for Breaker.

Breaker claiming u makes C a zero position. After Maker claims u, the residual game is exactly C-u. Indeed, |C-u|≥2 and every nontrivial cograph contains twins a,b. Apply Theorem 13 both in C after u is Maker-owned and in C-u, virtually assigning a to Maker and b to Breaker. Vertex u is then spoiled by b, while every vertex of C-u is happy in C exactly when it is happy in C-u. Thus Maker opening u exposes its child forest; Breaker taking u deletes its entire rooted tree. A prize leaf scores one only when Maker takes it.

Conversely, realize any rooted tree recursively: a prize leaf is K1; for an internal node, take the disjoint union of its child graphs and a zero K2 ballast, then join one new vertex to everything. That vertex is uniquely universal. The construction is a cograph and has linear size. Therefore the two decision problems are polynomially interreducible.

results.claim: The cograph game is linear-time solvable when every tree in the reduced forest has outdegree at most two.
results.proof_sketch: There are only two relevant equivalence types. Let A denote a prize leaf and Z the zero game. Induct upward. A node whose children contain zero A-types has game {0|0}=Z. With one A-child, Maker opening it leaves Breaker to move on A, yielding zero; Breaker can delete it, so both starting scores are zero and Theorem 6 gives Z. With two A-children, their sum is the constant game 1: two prize leaves score one regardless of starter. Hence the parent has options “Maker obtains 1” and “Breaker obtains 0,” exactly the game A. Z-children may be omitted. Labeling nodes bottom-up therefore leaves z copies of A at the top. Their scores are ceil(z/2) for Maker-first and floor(z/2) for Breaker-first.

results.claim: Reduced forests of height one—equivalently, disjoint unions of stars and isolated vertices after zero components are removed—admit an O(n^2) exact algorithm.
results.proof_sketch:
Let k1≤⋯≤kr be the leaf counts of unopened stars and let l be the number of exposed prize leaves. Write M(i,l),B(i,l) for the values with stars k1,…,ki remaining. An exchange induction shows that, among star moves, both players may restrict attention to the largest ki: Breaker preferentially deletes it, while Maker preferentially opens it. For j≤k, replacing an unopened j-star by a k-star cannot hurt Maker; moreover, with Breaker next, exposing k leaves while retaining the j-star is at least as favorable to Maker as exposing j leaves while retaining the k-star. Inspecting deletion, opening, and exposed-leaf moves proves these inequalities inductively.

Consequently,
M(i,l)=max(1+B(i,l-1) if l>0, B(i-1,l+ki)),
B(i,l)=min(M(i,l-1) if l>0, M(i-1,l)).
The bases are M(0,l)=ceil(l/2), B(0,l)=floor(l/2). Only states satisfying l+sum_{j≤i}kj≤K, where K=sum kj plus the initial exposed leaves, are needed. Filling by increasing i and l costs O(rK)=O(n^2).

results.claim: If q is the number of vertices of outdegree at least three in a reduced rooted forest, every residual forest occurring in play is equivalent, up to the integer score already secured, to a branching-core state (S,l), where l counts prize-leaf games and S is an antichain of at most q original nodes, each rooting a remaining component that contains a branching vertex.
results.proof_sketch:
Mark each original node whose rooted subtree contains a vertex of outdegree at least three. Any unmarked rooted subtree has maximum outdegree two, so the preceding bottom-up theorem replaces it, in every disjoint context, by A or by zero. Apply this replacement to every unmarked component initially and whenever Maker exposes children.

The components not replaced have roots S that form an antichain in the original forest. Their subtrees are disjoint, and each contains at least one of the q branching vertices; choosing one such vertex from each subtree injects S into those q vertices, so |S|≤q. If Maker opens v∈S, remove v, add its marked children to S, and add one to l for each unmarked child of A-type; zero-type children disappear. If Breaker chooses v, its component disappears. Choosing an A-type component either scores one and removes it for Maker or merely removes it for Breaker. These are all legal moves, so (S,l) preserves both starting-player scores exactly.

results.claim: The rooted-forest game, and hence SHVG on cographs, has an exact XP algorithm parameterized by q, the number of outdegree-at-least-three vertices in the reduced forest; in particular it is polynomial-time solvable for every fixed q.
results.proof_sketch:
For v∈S, precompute E(v), its children whose subtrees contain a branching vertex, and a(v), the number of its other children having A-type. Memoize
M(S,l)=max({1+B(S,l-1):l>0}∪{B((S\{v})∪E(v),l+a(v)):v∈S}),
B(S,l)=min({M(S,l-1):l>0}∪{M(S\{v},l):v∈S}),
with M(∅,0)=B(∅,0)=0. The first option in each recurrence is the prize-leaf move; the remaining options enumerate every active root. A measure given by the total number of original nodes in the active subtrees plus l strictly decreases, so memoization is acyclic.

There are at most (n+1)∑_{i=0}^q binom(n,i) states: l≤n and S is a subset of at most q original nodes. Each state has at most q+1 choices, and sorted q-node tuples support a transition in O(q+1) time. Thus time is O((q+1)^2(n+1)∑_{i=0}^q binom(n,i)) and space is O((n+1)∑_{i=0}^q binom(n,i)), both n^{O(q)}. The cotree-to-forest reduction and preprocessing are polynomial.

results.claim: The pair of standalone scores (Ms,Bs) is insufficient as a cotree dynamic-programming state.
results.proof_sketch: Both P3 and K1,3 have standalone scores (1,0). Nevertheless, P3+P3 has scores (1,1), whereas the height-one recurrence gives P3+K1,3 scores (2,1). Thus these components have identical left and right stops but different behavior in sums. Any full cotree algorithm must retain information richer than the two starting-player scores.

results.claim: For every m≥1, the rooted stars S_{2m} and S_{2m+1} have the same standalone scores (m,0), but adjoining one prize leaf A gives scores (m,1) and (m+1,1), respectively.
results.proof_sketch: A forest of t prize leaves has scores (ceil(t/2),floor(t/2)); in particular A+A has both scores 1 and is contextually the constant 1 by Theorem 6. Maker starting S_k must open its root and then receives the Breaker-first value of k prize leaves, while Breaker starting deletes the root. Hence S_{2m} and S_{2m+1} both have (m,0). In A+S_k, Maker either takes A for 1 or opens S_k and leaves Breaker on k+1 prizes; Breaker either deletes A and leaves Maker on S_k or deletes S_k and leaves Maker on A. Substitution gives (Ms,Bs)(A+S_{2m})=(m,1) and (Ms,Bs)(A+S_{2m+1})=(m+1,1). Thus the parent’s m=1 separator persists at every score scale.

results.claim: For every N there are N pairwise contextually inequivalent rooted-tree games on at most 2N+4 forest nodes that all have standalone scores (1,0); thus the failure of the (Ms,Bs) state is unbounded.
results.proof_sketch:
Define F_m to be a root with children A,A,S_{2m}; it has 2m+4 nodes. Breaker deletes its root for zero, while Maker opens it and leaves Breaker on 1+S_{2m}, whose Breaker-first score is 1. Hence every F_m has scores (1,0).

For 1≤r≤s, use S_{2s} as a context. Breaker starting on F_r+S_{2s} deletes one root, so the value is min(Ms(S_{2s}),Ms(F_r))=min(s,1)=1. Maker can open S_{2s}, giving s+Bs(F_r)=s, or open F_r, giving 1+Bs(S_{2r}+S_{2s}). With Breaker next on the two stars, deletion of one leaves Maker starting the other, so this latter Breaker score is min(r,s)=r. Therefore Ms(F_r+S_{2s})=max(s,r+1): it is s when r<s and s+1 when r=s. Thus, for r<s, the context S_{2s} distinguishes F_r from F_s. Taking m=1,…,N proves the claim. This is an information obstruction to score-pair summaries, not a hardness proof.

final_writeup:
A complete complexity classification is still not obtained, but the exact reductions and algorithms survive audit, and an unbounded obstruction now sharpens why a naïve cotree summary cannot finish the problem.

First reduce a cograph G exactly to the open-or-delete rooted-forest game. Connected components with either no universal vertex or at least two universal vertices have explicit pairing dominating sets and are zero games. A singleton becomes a prize leaf. A remaining connected component has a unique universal vertex u; it becomes an internal root over the recursively reduced components of C-u. Maker opening an internal root exposes its children, Breaker choosing a root deletes its whole subtree, and Maker taking a prize leaf scores one. The inverse construction realizes every rooted forest by cographs with linear overhead.

The verified tractable cases remain: maximum outdegree two is solvable in linear time because each subtree is equivalent to either a prize leaf A or zero, and height-one forests have the O(n^2) largest-star recurrence.

Let q be the number of reduced-forest vertices having outdegree at least three. Mark a node when its subtree contains such a branching vertex. Every unmarked subtree has maximum outdegree two and can therefore be replaced contextually by A or zero. After separating points already secured, any residual position consists of l copies of A and an antichain S of active roots whose disjoint subtrees each contain a branching vertex. Hence |S|≤q.

For each active root v, let E(v) be its marked children and let a(v) count its unmarked A-type children. The exact recurrences are

M(S,l)=max({1+B(S,l-1):l>0}∪{B((S\{v})∪E(v),l+a(v)):v∈S}),
B(S,l)=min({M(S,l-1):l>0}∪{M(S\{v},l):v∈S}).

They enumerate every legal move and terminate because every transition decreases the remaining original-node measure. Since l≤n and |S|≤q, memoization uses at most (n+1)∑_{i=0}^q binom(n,i) states and n^{O(q)} time. Thus SHVG on cographs is polynomial-time solvable whenever q is fixed.

The obstruction is stronger than one exceptional pair. The rooted stars S_{2m} and S_{2m+1} have identical standalone scores (m,0), but a prize-leaf context distinguishes them for every m. More sharply, let F_m have a root whose children are two prize leaves and S_{2m}. Every F_m has standalone scores (1,0), yet the games F_1,F_2,… are pairwise contextually inequivalent. For r<s, adjoining S_{2s} gives Maker-first score s with F_r but s+1 with F_s; the Breaker-first score is 1 in both cases. Thus for every N, N inequivalent component types with the same two stops already occur on O(N) nodes. Any exact compositional cotree algorithm must retain unbounded information beyond (Ms,Bs). This establishes a precise limitation, but not a complexity lower bound.

The unrestricted target remains open here: q can grow with n, the algorithm is XP rather than polynomial for unbounded q, and the contextual-type obstruction supplies neither a polynomial-time algorithm nor a matching hardness reduction. The requested classification is therefore only partially resolved.
